chunks: "The weakest link in most buck converters is the electrolytic capacitor, so I'd start there.
The electrolyte slowly evaporates, especially when hot and with high ripple current, so capacitance drops and ESR rises.
A common rule is that life doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius cooler.

As ESR climbs, output ripple goes up in proportion, transient droop gets worse, the capacitor runs hotter from its own ripple heating, and eventually the loop margin changes because the ESR zero moves.
If it's all ceramic, there's little wear-out, but class II ceramics lose a few percent capacitance per decade of time, and board flex can crack them into shorts.
The inductor is usually robust, but heat ages the winding insulation and some powdered cores increase their loss over time, and a saturation margin that was thin gets thinner when hot.
The silicon and the package can degrade through thermal cycling: bond wires and solder joints fatigue, die-attach thermal resistance rises, so the part runs hotter, and R DS(on) can drift up.
Gate oxide and hot-carrier effects are small in well-derated parts.
Net result: ripple rises, efficiency drops slightly, the loop moves, and eventually there's a start-up failure or a short.
I'd design for it by derating voltage and temperature, using polymer or ceramic capacitors where possible, keeping ripple current under the rating, and testing with accelerated life tests."
